node-1.label: Patient presented with sudden loss of consciousness and foaming at the mouth

node-2.label: Patient is in their 60s; complained of chest discomfort for the past 1 month and was taking Chinese medicine; drank about 180 mL of Chinese herbal medicine 20 minutes before developing syncope; vomit had a pale yellow color

node-3.label: Patient had no history of arrhythmias and no family history of sudden unexpected death or fatal cerebrovascular accident

node-4.label: Physical examination showed temperature 36°C, heart rate 124 beats/min, blood pressure 55/32 mm Hg, pulse oximetry 99% on room air, pupils 3 mm in diameter and reactive to light, skin cool moist and cyanosed, lung fields clear, and heart sounds indistinguishable due to tachycardia

why.why: Expert analysis explicitly confirms that blood aconitine positivity, bidirectional ventricular tachycardia with AV dissociation, and markedly elevated troponin T and BNP establish aconitine-induced cardiotoxicity as the cause of cardiovascular collapse. This mechanism directly explains the sudden loss of consciousness, foaming, vomiting, and shock, so acute cardiovascular collapse is the confirmed clinical presentation with a now-identified toxin-mediated cause.

Expert analysis confirms that positive blood aconitine, the characteristic ECG pattern of bidirectional ventricular tachycardia with AV dissociation, and elevated cardiac biomarkers are diagnostic of aconitine-induced cardiotoxicity. Combined with recent ingestion of 180 mL of Chinese herbal medicine 20 minutes before syncope and vomiting, this establishes herbal medicine toxicity with near certainty.

Expert analysis explicitly refutes primary seizure as the cause: the foaming at the mouth is explained by toxin-induced cardiovascular collapse, blood aconitine is positive, and ECG shows bidirectional ventricular tachycardia with AV dissociation. There is no primary neurological evidence, so seizure/convulsive syncope is effectively ruled out.

Expert analysis confirms that the arrhythmia is toxin-induced, as shown by positive blood aconitine and bidirectional ventricular tachycardia with AV dissociation, rather than a primary electrical event. The absence of prior arrhythmia and negative family history further refute a primary arrhythmic event, so confidence is reduced to 0.01.

node-9.label: ECG shows wide QRS tachycardia with alternating axis and AV dissociation (bidirectional ventricular tachycardia)

node-13.label: Follow-up ECG shows Q waves and T wave inversion indicating myocardial injury

node-14.label: Aconitine-induced cardiotoxicity (herbal medicine poisoning) is the cause of the patient's cardiovascular collapse

why.why: Expert analysis states that blood aconitine positivity, ECG showing bidirectional ventricular tachycardia with AV dissociation, and markedly elevated troponin T and BNP confirm aconitine-induced cardiotoxicity as the cause of cardiovascular collapse. This synthesis of the patient's herbal ingestion, vomiting, shock, and syncope makes the diagnosis nearly certain, with only echocardiography and herbal composition details still outstanding.

node-15.label: Aconitine-induced cardiotoxicity has caused secondary myocardial injury

attrs.why: Blood aconitine is positive and the ECG shows bidirectional ventricular tachycardia; troponin T and BNP are markedly elevated, and follow-up ECG shows Q waves with T wave inversion indicating myocardial injury. Expert analysis confirms aconitine-induced cardiotoxicity, and these findings together support secondary myocardial injury as a complication of the poisoning. Confidence is 0.85 because echocardiography is unavailable and the relative contributions of direct toxin-mediated injury versus shock-related ischemia are not fully quantified.
